title: Identifying Dominant Environmental Predictors of Coastal Shallow Groundwater Levels Across Diel to Seasonal Time Scales
content:
Abstract

Coastal zone, especially mega-deltas are densely populated and socioeconomically important, where shallow groundwater responds to interacting terrestrial, marine, atmospheric and engineered influences across multiple time scales, contributing to uncertainty in groundwater prediction. Here, we utilized a multiscale information-theoretic diagnostic framework to analyze groundwater-level (GWL) dynamics in the Yellow River Delta and to identifying dominant environmental predictors of coastal shallow groundwater levels across diel to seasonal time scales. Results indicate that: (a) the seasonal component dominates GWL variability, accounting for 73% of total variance. Air temperature (T) serves as the primary predictor at sites closer to the coastline, whereas precipitation (P) dominates at sites farther inland. Seasonal GWL is asynchronous with T and P, with offsets of 27 ± 23 and 13 days, respectively. (b) the multiday component accounts for 25% of total variance; here, evaporative demand drives recession dynamics, while P induces episodic recharge pulses (lag: 1.1 ± 0.25 days). (c) the diel component (2% of variance) exhibits regular diel cycles. P outperforms potential evapotranspiration (PET) as the dominant predictor, suggesting that rapid infiltration events generate intense high-frequency hydraulic signals that outweigh regular diel evapotranspiration oscillations in information content. Near tidal channels, tides dominate, with GWL lagging tidal stage by 4 hr. By explicitly resolving time-scale dependence, asynchrony, and nonlinearity, this study advances the understanding of coastal shallow GWL dynamics and provides a basis for GWL prediction, model development, and coastal groundwater management.
